content: Perinatal mortality, also referred to as perinatal death, describes the death of a fetus or neonate and serves as the basis for calculating the perinatal mortality rate. The exact definition of perinatal mortality varies, particularly regarding whether early fetal deaths and late neonatal deaths are included or excluded. For instance, the World Health Organization (WHO) defines perinatal mortality as deaths occurring during late pregnancy (at 22 completed weeks of gestation and beyond), during childbirth, and up to seven completed days of life. However, this definition is not universally accepted. Perinatal mortality is the combined total of fetal mortality and neonatal mortality. Fetal mortality refers to stillbirths or fetal deaths, encompassing any death of a fetus after 20 weeks of gestation or weighing 500 grams or more. Some definitions of perinatal mortality exclude early fetal mortality (occurring between 20 and 27 weeks of gestation) and include only late fetal deaths and neonatal deaths. Fetal deaths can be further categorized into deaths occurring before labor, known as antenatal (antepartum) deaths, and deaths occurring during labor, referred to as intranatal (intrapartum) deaths. Fetal mortality can be reduced through optimal preconception health in women prior to pregnancy. Neonatal mortality is divided into early neonatal mortality, which refers to the death of a live-born infant within the first seven days of life, and late neonatal mortality, which covers deaths occurring after seven days but before 29 days of life. The sum of these two categories constitutes neonatal mortality. Some definitions of perinatal mortality include only early neonatal mortality. Neonatal mortality is influenced by the quality of in-hospital care provided to the neonate. Both neonatal mortality and postneonatal mortality (which accounts for deaths during the remaining 11 months of the first year of life) are reflected in the infant mortality rate. The perinatal mortality rate (PNMR) is defined as the number of perinatal deaths per 1,000 total births and is typically reported on an annual basis. It is a critical indicator used to evaluate the quality of healthcare delivery. However, comparisons of PNMRs between different regions or populations may be complicated by variations in definitions, registration biases, and differences in the underlying risk factors of the populations being studied. PNMRs vary significantly, with rates below 10 in some developed countries and rates more than 10 times higher in certain developing countries. The WHO has not published contemporary data on this topic.
